title: Imaginary World
goal: Your kid invents a whole world: what the land looks like, who lives there, how they live together and the legends they tell. Then they map it, build one corner of it, and give a tour to someone who's never been there.
need: Clay or playdough, small figurines or natural objects for scale
Outdoor option: sticks, rocks, mud, leaves and sand for the model

lesson.text: A world feels real when everything follows from one big idea. Ten random cool things feel like a pile, not a place.
lesson.before: There are dragons, a castle, a rainbow sea and robots.

model.line: In my world, there's no night. The sun never sets.
So the ground never cools. People live in caves and deep forests for shade.
Creatures have thick eyelids to sleep in bright light.
A bell tells everyone when to sleep, because there's no dark to do it.

lesson.modelNote: One strong idea, and everything else follows from it. That's the question behind every step: why is it like that?

howTo.intro: You don't need teaching experience. You're the curious traveller, not the designer. Ask 'what would I see if I stepped off a boat here?' instead of suggesting answers. The world can be as weird as they like. It doesn't need to be realistic, just consistent.

plan.what: Pick the world and design the land and who lives there (Steps 1 and 2).
Build the culture and rules, then map it (Steps 3 and 4).
Build one corner, tell a legend and give the tour (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: They want to put in everything they love from books and movies
troubleshoot.a: Ask 'what's YOUR thing that nobody else's world has?' Borrowed pieces can stay, as long as they fit the big idea.
The legend can be told out loud, drawn as a comic or recorded. Jot down the key points while they talk.

skills.name: Storytelling
skills.text: legends with a reason behind them

skills.name: Explaining
skills.text: a world someone else can picture

steps.title: Pick the world and its big idea
steps.why: One strong idea is better than ten vague ones.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a world type from the World types card in the Worldbuilder's Toolkit at the end of the guide: a planet, a hidden land, a floating world, a tiny world. Then they name the one big difference from Earth, like no night, water that flows up or sound you can see.
steps.you: Help them commit to one idea before building everything at once. Ask what their world has that nobody else's does.
ask: If you could tell someone one thing about your world, what would it be?
What's the first thing a visitor would notice?
steps.tip: Test the big idea: does it change daily life? 'Everything is purple' doesn't. 'There's no night' changes when people sleep, where they live and what grows.

levels.explore: Pick a world type and draw the big difference.
levels.develop: Write the big difference and 3 ways it changes daily life.
levels.extend: Work out what the big difference does to the weather, the food and how people travel.

steps.title: Design the land and who lives there
steps.why: Where creatures live should explain how they live.
steps.kid: Your kid sketches a rough layout with at least 3 regions and any strange terrain: crystal fields, fog forests, lava plains. Then they fill it with creatures or groups: what they look like, what they eat, whether they're friendly or dangerous, and how they get around.
steps.you: Connect the land to the life with one question: 'Why do they live there and not over there?'
ask: How does the land change how the creatures live?
What's the most dangerous place in your world?
steps.tip: Creatures should fit where they live. A fire-breathing animal in the ice region needs a really good reason.

levels.explore: Draw 3 regions and one creature for each.
levels.develop: Draw 3 or more regions, with creatures that fit them, and explain why.
levels.extend: Show how creatures depend on each other: who eats what, who trades with whom.

steps.title: Build the culture and the rules
steps.why: Every world needs a way of living together.
steps.kid: Your kid decides how the people or creatures organise themselves (one leader, a council, no leader, something unusual), what they value most, and 2 or 3 rules everyone follows, each with a reason. Then they invent a consequence for breaking a rule that fits their world.
steps.you: Ask 'why?' a lot. The sentence you're after is 'They have that rule because...'
ask: What does a regular day look like for someone there?
What would shock a visitor from our world?
steps.tip: Push past 'they go to jail.' A society of sky-dwellers might ground someone, literally: no flying for a week.

levels.explore: Say who's in charge and one rule.
levels.develop: Write how they organise, what they value and 3 rules with reasons.
levels.extend: Add a disagreement between two groups and how their rules settle it.

steps.title: Map it and build one corner
steps.why: A map makes it a place. A model makes it real.
steps.kid: Your kid makes the real map: every region, where each group lives, important places, place names and a compass rose. Then they build the most interesting corner in 3D: a shoebox diorama, a clay landscape, a block city, or outside with sticks, mud and sand.
steps.you: Help with materials and anything that won't stay together. Let them direct.
ask: Which part of your world would you most want to visit?
What detail makes the model feel like it belongs in your world?
steps.tip: Make one corner feel real instead of building everything. A shoebox is plenty.

levels.explore: Draw a map with names and build one small piece.
levels.develop: Draw a full map using the Map checklist card, and build one corner in 3D.
levels.extend: Add a scale (1 cm = 10 km) and work out the travel distance between 2 places.

steps.title: Tell a legend and give the tour
steps.why: Stories explain the world, and the tour tests if it holds together.
steps.kid: Your kid invents one legend that explains something they built: why a region is forbidden, or how the river got its colour. They tell it, write it or draw it. Then they give a tour to someone who's never been there: the big idea, the map, the model and the legend.
steps.you: Listen to the legend without editing it. On the tour, be a real traveller and ask the questions from the Traveller's questions card.
ask: What happened in your world before the legend starts?
What would you add if you had another week?
steps.tip: A question they can't answer isn't a failure. It's the next thing to invent.

levels.explore: Tell a short legend out loud and show the map.
levels.develop: Write or draw the legend, and give a full tour.
levels.extend: Film the tour, and answer all 5 traveller's questions without stopping to invent.

after.label: Worldbuilding rules
lines: One big idea, and everything follows from it.
Every creature fits where it lives.
Every legend explains something you built.

conclusion.headline: Their world exists now.
conclusion.text: Your kid did what writers, game designers and filmmakers spend years learning: they built a world that holds together. They connected the land to the life, invented a culture with reasons behind its rules, told a legend that explains it, and showed it to someone clearly enough to make them believe in it.
conclusion.celebrate: Tell them which part pulled you in: the big idea, a creature that fit its home perfectly, or the legend.
extensions: Write a longer story set in the world: a quest, a mystery, a day in the life
Make a travel guide or field journal with drawings
Invent a board game set in the world, with the Board Game Studio guide

signs: They ask 'but why?' about worlds in books and movies
They notice how land and weather shape how people live
They explain their ideas so others can picture them
makeItReal: Next time you travel or read about a new place, ask them what the land makes people there do: what they eat, how they build, how they get around. Real places follow the same rules as their world.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.
